narrative:
The model predicted a 63.8% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. First, your family income bracket of Middle had the strongest influence and pushed the prediction toward failure. Although many accepted students also come from middle-income families, this characteristic is associated overall with a higher risk of not passing the bar on the first try. Second, your first-year law school performance placed you in the 5th decile, noticeably below the average of 6th decile among accepted students; this weaker early performance also pulled the prediction toward failure. Third, your LSAT score of 39 was actually helpful, sitting above the accepted-student average of 37.2; this higher score worked in your favor and nudged the outcome toward passing, but it was not enough to overcome the other two factors.

In short, your middle-income background and especially your below-average first-year grades were the main reasons the model saw an elevated risk of bar exam failure. Your stronger LSAT and solid third-year decile helped, yet not sufficiently to reach the required confidence level for admission.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening your first-year academic record if you retake courses or enroll elsewhere, and consider reaching out to the admissions office to discuss how to improve your profile for future applications.
